questions.prompt: What is the capital city of Libya?

hints.nudge: A capital city is where a country’s government meets. The other three are capital cities too, of other countries.
hints.whereToLook: Look in the “Geography” part of the Libya article.

questions.proof: The capital of Libya is Tripoli, which is a port on the sea.

questions.prompt: Which of these countries shares a border with Libya?

hints.nudge: Two countries are neighbours when you can walk from one into the other. Picture Libya on the globe and look at what it touches.
hints.whereToLook: Look in the opening paragraphs of the Libya article.

questions.proof: It is bordered by the Mediterranean Sea to the north, Egypt to the east, Sudan to the southeast, Chad and Niger to the south, and Algeria and Tunisia to the west.

questions.prompt: Which language is an official language of Libya?

hints.nudge: An official language is the one used in schools, courts and government. The other three are spoken in other countries.
hints.whereToLook: Look in the “Great Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya” part of the Libya article.

questions.proof: In 1977 Libya became "Al-Jamahiriya al-`Arabiyah al-Libiyah ash-Sha`biyah al-Ishtirakiyah al-Uzma" (Arabic: الجماهيرية العربية الليبية الشعبية الاشتراكية العظمة).
questions.proofSection: Great Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya

questions.prompt: What money is used in Libya?

hints.nudge: Money names often come from a country’s own words. The other three are spent in other countries.
hints.whereToLook: Look in the “Economy” part of the Libya article.

questions.proof: The money of Libya is called the Libyan dinar.

questions.prompt: Fill the gap: “After World War II, the regions of Libya were ruled by military governors from both Britain and _____.”

hints.nudge: In the sentence the missing word sits beside “Britain”. It names one thing, not an action.
hints.whereToLook: Look in the “United Kingdom of Libya” part of the Libya article.

questions.proof: After World War II, the regions of Libya were ruled by military governors from both Britain and France.
